paper_title: Self-Play Search Distillation for Large Language Model Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Improving reasoning abilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) requires high-quality data that exposes difficult decisions, competing alternatives, and their consequences. Data scarcity is driven by the low quality of synthetic data and the cost of human labeling. We introduce Self-Play Search Distillation (SPSD), a framework for generating superhuman synthetic data via self-play of MuZero-like networks trained on board games. SPSD uses executable environments to turn search into structured reasoning problems. At each state, the expert identifies a preferred decision, plausible alternatives, plausible opponent replies, and value estimates. By converting the self-play search records into superhuman chains-of-thought, we train LLMs with environment-grounded supervision. Although trained only on self-play search records, SPSD transfers to unseen mathematics. On Qwen3-4B-Base, it raises the mean over six mathematics benchmarks from 24.1 to 36.6 while increasing the held-out-game win rate from 15% to 45%. SPSD offers an annotation-efficient way to create high-quality synthetic data for improving LLM performance in reasoning tasks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Scaling the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) requires more than simply increasing the amount of training data. It requires synthetic supervision whose quality can exceed the students current capabilities. Final answers reveal whether solution succeeded, but not how the solver preserved state, rejected plausible alternatives, or anticipated delayed consequences (Li et al., 2023; Nanda et al., 2023; Valmeekam et al., 2023a,b). Human process supervision can expose these operations, but it is costly to collect, difficult to verify, and ultimately bounded by the expertise of its annotators (Ouyang et al., 2022). Recent self-generation methods offer scalable alternative by allowing the learner to construct tasks, traces, or feedback (Chen et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025). Yet, when the learner itself participates in generating the supervision, data quality remains coupled to its current errors and limitations. The central challenge is to generate structured supervision that exposes comparisons and consequences beyond the students current policy and can be checked independently. Executable board games provide compact testbed for this challenge. Their rules define exact transitions and legal actions, and terminal outcomes expose delayed consequences, while controlled rule changes vary the reasoning problem without changing the evaluation interface. Search-based self-play systems in this lineage have achieved superhuman play and, crucially, retain more than the selected action: they expose alternatives, opponent replies, branch values, and replayable consequences (Silver et al., 2017a; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021). single root search can therefore provide preferred action, distribution over legal alternatives, branch values, and continuations that can be checked independently by replay. These records capture the comparisons and delayed consequences absent from outcome-only game logs. Crucially, search-based self-play has already demonstrated that such experts can surpass human performance, providing source of supervision that is not inherently capped by human expertise (Silver et al., 2017a; Schrittwieser et al., 2020). By placing these external search expertsrather than the LLM itselfin the data-generation loop, we decouple supervision quality from the students current policy. Self-play search thus becomes more than game-playing mechanism. It provides programmable source of search-derived reasoning traces whose alternatives and consequences can be checked by replay under the executable rules of each environment. We introduce Self-Play Search Distillation (SPSD), an offline bridge from superhumancapable self-play search to LLM post-training. Given search expert, SPSD converts replayable decision states into verifier-grounded supervision that exposes the selected action, plausible alternatives, and their consequences, together with complementary questions about the underlying state. The LLM never participates in expert self-play during post-training and receives no search information at inference time. Our experiments show that SPSD can improve mathematical reasoning while preserving game competence, although the magnitude of the gains depends on the backbone. We make three contributions. 1 We introduce an offline framework that turns self-play search into scalable source of replaygrounded supervision for LLM reasoning. 2 We develop replay-grounded interface that converts expert decisions, alternatives, and state transitions into reasoning traces and six complementary state-supervision tasks. 3 We evaluate whether this supervision transfers beyond the source search environments, across game play, controlled rule variation, and mathematical reasoning.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Game reasoning. Executable games support both the evaluation of stateful reasoning and the generation of interaction-grounded supervision. ChessGPT (Feng et al., 2023) connects policy learning with language modeling, while ChessBench (Ruoss et al., 2024) evaluates chess prediction against engine-derived targets. Training on complete games (Zhang et al., 2025) examines whether full-game context improves chess play, latent-state analyses (Karvonen, 2024) probe internal board representations, and chess reasoning testbeds (Wang et al., 2025) evaluate state tracking and tactical reasoning. GTBench (Duan et al., 2024) evaluates strategic reasoning across gametheoretic settings, while lmgame-Bench (Hu et al., 2025) studies interactive play and transfer from game training. KORGym (Shi et al., 2025) and TextArena (Guertler et al., 2025) provide multiturn game collections that support evaluation and training. LLM-guided MCTS (Guo et al., 2024) uses language models to prune actions and estimate state values, while Schultz et al. (2025) compares explicit MCTS with search generated inside the language model. While these approaches primarily evaluate game competence, train game-playing policies, or place the language model inside the planning loop, we train search expert separately and let it export environment-grounded root decisions, alternatives, and continuations as offline language-model supervision. Synthetic supervision. Synthetic methods derive supervision from verifiable tasks and explicit solution processes. AlphaGeometry (Trinh et al., 2024) generates synthetic theorems and proofs without human demonstrations, Enigmata (Chen et al., 2025) pairs controllable puzzles with rule-based verifiers, and Absolute Zero (Zhao et al., 2025) lets one model propose and solve executable reasoning tasks under programmatic feedback. LogicPuzzleRL (Wong et al., 2025) trains with verifier rewards on logic puzzles, while Reasoning Gym (Stojanovski et al., 2025) provides procedurally generated reasoning environments with verifiable rewards. Complementary lines of work expose intermediate computation rather than only final outcomes. Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) elicits stepwise rationales, Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023) searches over alternative thoughts at inference, and ASTRO (Kim et al., 2025) trains on natural-language MCTS traces with reflection and backtracking. Procedure cloning (Yang et al., 2022) imitates expert computations, while Stream of Search (Gandhi et al., 2024) bootstraps from flattened search trajectories. RLoT (Hao et al., 2025) learns adaptive reasoning control through inference-time reinforcement learning, and ToTRL (Wu et al., 2025) reinforces treestructured reasoning through puzzle solving. Algorithm Distillation (Laskin et al., 2023) models learning histories to induce in-context policy improvement. Studies of Othello sequence models (Li et al., 2023; Nanda et al., 2023) probe latent board-state representations, while PlanBench (Valmeekam et al., 2023a) and related critical planning evaluation (Valmeekam et al., 2023b) test plan generation and reasoning about change. SPSD also transfers structured decision information, but it supervises one root decision from planning expert. It retains ranked alternatives and replayable continuations that justify the selected action without exposing the full search tree or asking the student to reproduce the planners internal computations. While game competence tracks mathematical accuracy across scale, even frontier models do not saturate on board-game reasoning. Self-play and post-training. Language-model post-training draws supervision from people, teachers, model generations, and executable environments. RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022) established preference-based posttraining, DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) optimizes preference pairs directly, and knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) transfers predictive behavior from teacher. Self-Instruct (Wang et al., 2023) bootstraps instruction data from model generations, while SPIN (Chen et al., 2024) iteratively contrasts target responses with responses produced by earlier model versions. Beyond Human Data (Singh et al., 2024) filters self-generated solutions using binary feedback, DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024) introduces GRPO for mathematical reasoning, ProRL (Liu et al., 2025b) studies prolonged reinforcement learning, and VersaPRM (Zeng et al., 2025) learns process rewards from synthetic reasoning data. SPIRAL (Liu et al., 2025a) directly optimizes an LLM through online multi-turn game self-play. OpenSIR (Kwan et al., 2025) alternates single policy between proposing and solving mathematical problems under difficultyand diversity-calibrated rewards, and SCOPE (Kwan et al., 2026) extends self-play to open-ended tasks by co-evolving task-proposing challenger with retrieval-augmented solver, graded by rubrics from judge model. Code-based self-play (Bachrach et al., 2025) refines executable game strategies through competition, while SPADE (Liu et al., 2026) co-evolves executable tasks and reasoning agent through hint-based regret. ALE (Bellemare et al., 2013), TextWorld (Côté et al., 2018), Procgen (Cobbe et al., 2020), Ludii (Piette et al., 2020), and OpenSpiel (Lanctot et al., 2019) provide automatically scored settings for interaction and training. POET (Wang et al., 2019), unsupervised environment design (Dennis et al., 2020), and regret-based environment design (Parker-Holder et al., 2022) instead adapt the task distribution as the learner changes. In SPSD, self-play is part of corpus construction. The decisions of the trained search experts are converted into an offline corpus. This shifts self-play from optimizing the learner to producing reusable, environment-grounded reasoning data.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: SPSD turns this intermediate representation into an offline bridge from self-play search to LLM posttraining. SPSD comprises three stages. search expert plays against itself and exports one record for each decision state it reaches. Each record is then replayed in the environment, and records whose fields cannot be reproduced are discarded. The surviving records are converted into prompts and reference responses. The expert is held fixed during generation, so the supervision it produces is independent of the student trained on it. For each source game we train an ExIt-family search expert (Anthony et al., 2017) and select training step, suppressing the ExIt iteration index to write the search outputs as πE, vE, and BE. sections.title: 5 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Training corpus and search experts. We construct the main SPSD corpus from Connect4, Domineering, Simplified Othello, and Tic-Tac-Chess to cover alignment under gravity, spatial blocking, line capture, and movement-based tactics. For each game, an EfficientZero expert (Ye et al., 2021) is trained by self-play through LightZero (Niu et al., 2023), with 50 MCTS simulations per decision during data generation. Each game contributes 5,000 examples, reduced to 600 for Tic-Tac-Chess by its smaller pool of verified states. Each game allocates 80% of its examples to move choice with replay-grounded reasoning and 20% to the six statequestion tasks, which receive equal quotas after pooling. Appendix details the allocation and verification criteria, and Appendix C.1 reports the expert-training settings. Models and post-training. We test pool of models spanning different families and types. Qwen3-4B-Base, Qwen3-8B with thinking disabled and enabled, and Llama-3.1-8B cover base, thinking, and instruction-tuned conditions across two families. SFT fits the linearized MCTS traces of the SPSD corpus directly, and OPSD supplies them as the privileged trace that conditions the teacher. RuleBot-Distill keeps the OPSD procedure unchanged and replaces the search-derived corpus with completions from the heuristic rule bot, leaving the origin of the supervision as the only difference between the two conditions. Every setting is trained for 1,000 optimization steps on one Nvidia H200 GPU with 141 GB. Appendices and detail the optimization, decoding, and compute settings. Prompting. For move-choice tasks, all conditions receive the game rules, current state, player to move, and legal actions, and return final action in the same boxed-answer format. State-question prompts use the same state representation and require the task-specific answer in box. Appendices and specify the move prompt and statequestion tasks. Rule diversity. To test the effect of rule diversity under fixed training budget, we compare curricula drawn from separate pool of five base games and nine variants per game, yielding 50 environments. Each variant changes local rule governing scoring, openings, movement, or winning conditions while preserving the observation shape, board topology, and action-space size. Appendix details the rule changes, and Appendix reports the composition and structural properties of these 50 environments. Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate game transfer on 15 held-out games from the Ludii collection (Piette et al., 2020), disjoint from the training environments. Appendices and E.1 describe the game selection and rules. The primary game metric is the mean FIDE score, assigning 0, 0.5, and 1 to losses, draws, and wins, respectively. Episode win rate and move legality are also reported, where legality is the fraction of scored attempts that produce valid legal action. Formatting, parsing, and illegal-action failures count as unsuccessful attempts. For out-of-domain transfer, we evaluate mathematics on MATH500, AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, Olympiad Bench, and Minerva Math. We use pass@1 for MATH500, Olympiad Bench, and Minerva Math, and average accuracy over 32 sampled responses per problem for AIME24, AIME25, and AMC23. Appendix specifies the sampling settings and generation limits for both evaluations. Search distillation analysis. To assess whether SPSD transfers the action-choice policy of MCTS into the LLM, which analyses candidate actions through the positions they lead to before committing to one, we follow Chen et al. (2026) and use GPT-5.6 to read each reasoning trace and recover the positions it considers and the move it commits to, expressed as legal actions of the game. Restoring the position the model faced at that turn and querying the expert of that game yields value for every legal move together with the move its search prefers. For each episode, Q50 averages the search values the expert assigns to the committed moves from the player-to-move perspective, over the turns for which it returns value. Oracle agreement measures how often the committed move matches the action the expert search prefers. Appendix C.2 reports the selection and aggregation protocol.

sections.title: 6 Results
sections.content: Our results support conditional view of search transfer. Search-derived supervision improves performance when the student can convert valueordered traces into decisions, and neither legality nor longer reasoning traces is sufficient on its own. Table 1, Figure 3, and Figure 4 expose this distinction across model conditions, throughout optimization, and under fresh search replay. RQHow does transfer vary across model families and decision metrics? Held-out games provide the central test of transfer beyond the training environments, where the model must choose actions in unfamiliar rule systems  (Table 1)  . For Qwen3-4B-Base, OPSD triples the held-out-game win rate from 15% to 45%. The corresponding FIDE score rises from 15% to 39.9%, while the model produces legal actions in 75.1% of the evaluated positions. Search-distilled guidance lets the model use ranked alternatives and their consequences when it encounters games outside the training environments. This knowledge transfers to mathematical reasoning, raising the six-benchmark mean from 24.1 to 36.6. sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: SPSD turns records produced by self-play search experts in executable environments into replaygrounded supervision for language-model posttraining. Each record combines the selected action with ranked alternatives, search values, and replayed continuations to support comparative move-choice traces, verified state questions, and OPSD along student-generated prefixes. Across the Qwen3-4B training budgets studied, OPSD provides the most stable overall performance improvements among the compared methods, while SFT loses earlier gains under longer training. The variant-enriched curriculum strengthens held-outgame performance and mathematical reasoning transfer through more diverse search-grounded supervision. SPSD opens direction for future work on continual training through expanding curricula of executable environments, with search experts generating supervision for new rules and decision problems.

sections.title: A Grounded MCTS Linearization
sections.content: To distill search reasoning abilities into the LLM, we linearize the records that the trained SPSD MuZero experts produce. For each decision state, non-terminal board position with the player to move and the legal actions available in it, the experts export one record. We state the recorded decision, its retained alternatives, and their consequences in natural language. Replay restores the recorded state and follows each retained branch, so every statement in the resulting trace follows from an observed transition. record m(s) stores the serialized environment state s, its legal-action set, the recorded target, the root policy and value outputs, and, for each exported root action, its canonical handle, visit count, export index, action-specific edge value or missing-value marker, and retained branch prefix. Numerical search telemetry selects which evidence to retain and never enters the trace. The record pairs the trace with the action sequence it replays, and only the trace reaches the student, ending with exactly one boxed legal handle. Replay validation. Restoring in the executable environment recomputes the board, active player, legal actions, and phase-specific fields. record is retained only when these fields agree with their serialized values and A(s). Failure to replay rejects the record, whereas failure to replay an optional alternative or reply removes only that branch from the trace. For every retained branch, replay records the legal action prefix, the recomputed successor states, and any terminal flag and outcome reached along the prefix. Branch selection and evidence gates. Each export contains at most eight root-action records. After excluding a, the exported legal action with the greatest visit count becomes aalt, with ties broken by export order. The corresponding edge value is Q(a) = r(s, a) + γσV (T (s, a)), expressed from the current root players perspective, where γ = 1 in this corpus, σ = 1 when the child changes player, and σ = +1 otherwise.
